::: {.callout-tip}
## In this chapter you will learn to

- describe a group with its **mean** and **standard deviation**
- read a **normal distribution**
- explain what a **p-value** and **alpha** mean
- run and read a **t-test**
:::

## The study

A lab wants to know whether people trust an **expressive** robot (it smiles, nods and uses your name) more than a **neutral** robot (same words, no expressions).

Forty visitors take part. Each person meets **one** robot, chats with it for five minutes, then answers *"How much do you trust this robot?"* on a slider from 0 to 100. Because each person sees only one robot, this is called a **between-subjects** design.

```{webr}
#| caption: Load the data
visits <- read.csv("data/robot_one_visit.csv")
head(visits)
```

Each row is one person. The code boxes on this page run in your browser: edit any of them and press **Run Code**. **Start Over** brings the original code back.

## The mean: the typical value

The **mean** is the sum of all values divided by how many values there are:

$$\bar{x} = \frac{x_1 + x_2 + \dots + x_n}{n}$$

```{webr}
#| caption: Group means
neutral    <- visits$trust[visits$robot == "neutral"]
expressive <- visits$trust[visits$robot == "expressive"]

mean(neutral)
mean(expressive)
mean(expressive) - mean(neutral)
```

The expressive group's mean is about 12 points higher. Is that a real difference, or could two groups differ this much just by luck? To answer that, we first need to know how much people's ratings **vary**.

## Variance and standard deviation: how spread out

Two groups can have the same mean but very different spread. The **variance** is the average squared distance from the mean:

$$s^2 = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}$$

The **standard deviation** (SD) is the square root of the variance. It is easier to read because it is in the same units as the data: trust points.

```{webr}
#| caption: Spread
var(neutral)
sd(neutral)
sd(expressive)

boxplot(trust ~ robot, data = visits, col = c("#92c5de", "#f4a582"),
        ylab = "Trust (0-100)", xlab = "")
stripchart(trust ~ robot, data = visits, vertical = TRUE,
           method = "jitter", add = TRUE, pch = 19)
```

The SDs are about 11 to 13 points: most people sit within roughly 12 points of their group's mean. The two groups overlap a lot, even though their means differ by about one SD. Keep that in mind: a difference in means does not mean everyone in one group scored higher.

## The normal distribution

Many measurements pile up around the mean and thin out evenly on both sides, making a bell-shaped curve called the **normal distribution**. Two numbers describe it completely: the **mean** sets its center and the **SD** sets its width.

A useful rule of thumb: about **68%** of values fall within 1 SD of the mean, and about **95%** within 2 SDs.

Move the sliders and watch the curve change.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof mu = Inputs.range([20, 80], {value: 55, step: 1, label: "Mean"})
viewof sigma = Inputs.range([4, 25], {value: 12, step: 1, label: "Standard deviation"})
```

```{webr}
#| caption: A normal distribution
#| input:
#|   - mu
#|   - sigma
#| runbutton: false
#| startover: false
#| fig-height: 4
curve(dnorm(x, mu, sigma), from = 0, to = 100, lwd = 2, n = 300,
      ylim = c(0, 0.1), xlab = "Trust (0-100)", ylab = "How common")
xs <- seq(mu - sigma, mu + sigma, length.out = 200)
polygon(c(xs, rev(xs)), c(dnorm(xs, mu, sigma), rep(0, 200)),
        col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.35), border = NA)
abline(v = mu, lty = 2)
title(sprintf("About 68%% of people fall between %d and %d", mu - sigma, mu + sigma))
```

Real data are never perfectly normal, especially in small groups. Here are our neutral-robot ratings:

```{webr}
#| caption: Is our data roughly normal?
#| fig-height: 4
hist(neutral, breaks = 8, col = "grey85", main = "Neutral robot", xlab = "Trust (0-100)")
```

Bumpy, but roughly one hill in the middle with no extreme values. That is close enough for the t-test below, which is fairly forgiving, especially as groups get larger.

## Could it be luck? The null hypothesis

Even if the robot made no difference at all, two random groups of 20 people would almost never have exactly the same mean. So we set up two competing ideas:

- **Null hypothesis (H₀):** the robots earn the same average trust. Our 12-point difference is just luck.
- **Alternative hypothesis (H₁):** the robots earn different average trust.

We can see what luck alone produces. If the robot did not matter, the "neutral" and "expressive" labels would be meaningless, so we can **shuffle** them and recalculate the difference. Doing that 2,000 times shows the range of differences that luck produces:

```{webr}
#| caption: What differences does luck produce?
#| fig-height: 4
observed <- mean(expressive) - mean(neutral)

set.seed(1)
shuffled_diffs <- replicate(2000, {
  fake_robot <- sample(visits$robot)   # shuffle the labels
  mean(visits$trust[fake_robot == "expressive"]) -
    mean(visits$trust[fake_robot == "neutral"])
})

hist(shuffled_diffs, breaks = 40, col = "grey85",
     main = "Differences when the robot does not matter",
     xlab = "Difference in mean trust (expressive - neutral)")
abline(v = c(-observed, observed), col = "red", lwd = 2)

# Share of shuffles at least as extreme as our real difference
mean(abs(shuffled_diffs) >= abs(observed))
```

The red lines mark our real difference (and its mirror image). Luck almost never produces a gap that large: only about 0.35% of shuffles did. That last number is a **p-value**.

## p-values and alpha

**The p-value** answers one question: *if the null hypothesis were true, how often would we see a difference at least this big?* A small p-value means our result would be surprising if the robot made no difference.

**Alpha (α)** is the cut-off you choose **before** looking at the data, usually **0.05**. If p < α, we reject the null hypothesis and call the result *statistically significant*.

Alpha is also the false-alarm rate you agree to accept. With α = 0.05, when there truly is no effect, about 1 study in 20 will still give p < 0.05 by luck. Let's check by running 1,000 pretend studies where both robots have exactly the same true mean:

```{webr}
#| caption: 1,000 studies with no real difference
#| fig-height: 4
set.seed(2)
p_values <- replicate(1000, {
  group_a <- rnorm(20, mean = 55, sd = 12)
  group_b <- rnorm(20, mean = 55, sd = 12)
  t.test(group_a, group_b)$p.value
})

mean(p_values < 0.05)   # share of false alarms

hist(p_values, breaks = 20, col = "grey85",
     main = "p-values when there is NO real difference", xlab = "p-value")
abline(v = 0.05, col = "red", lwd = 2)
```

About 5% of the studies came out "significant" even though nothing was going on. These false alarms are called **Type I errors**.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Three common mistakes

1. **"p = 0.003 means there is a 0.3% chance the null hypothesis is true."** No. The p-value assumes the null is true and asks how surprising the data are.
2. **"p > 0.05 proves there is no difference."** No. It means this study could not tell. A bigger study might.
3. **"Significant means important."** No. Always look at the size of the difference too: 12 points on a 100-point scale.
:::

## The t-test

The shuffle idea works, but there is a classic shortcut: the **t-test**. It divides the difference in means by its **standard error** (SE), which is how much the difference would wobble from sample to sample:

$$t = \frac{\bar{x}_{expressive} - \bar{x}_{neutral}}{SE}, \qquad SE = \sqrt{\frac{s^2_{expressive}}{n_{expressive}} + \frac{s^2_{neutral}}{n_{neutral}}}$$

A big t means the difference is large compared with the wobble. The SE gets smaller when people vary less, or when there are more people.

```{webr}
#| caption: t by hand, then with t.test()
se <- sqrt(var(expressive) / 20 + var(neutral) / 20)
c(difference = observed, se = se, t = observed / se)

t.test(trust ~ robot, data = visits)
```

How to read the output:

- **t = 3.20**: the difference is about 3 standard errors away from zero.
- **df ≈ 37**: degrees of freedom, roughly the number of people minus 2. R's default (Welch's t-test) adjusts it slightly so the groups don't need equal variances.
- **p-value = 0.003**: below α = 0.05, so we reject the null hypothesis. It also matches our shuffle result.
- **95% confidence interval: 4.3 to 19.4**: the range of true differences that fit our data.

A t-test relies on three things:

1. **Independence:** each value comes from a different, unrelated person. *Chapter 2 is about what happens when this breaks.*
2. **Roughly normal values** in each group. This matters less as groups get larger.
3. **Numbers with equal steps:** the gap from 40 to 50 means the same as from 80 to 90. *Chapter 4 is about rating scales where this may not hold.*

**Writing it up:** *Visitors trusted the expressive robot more (M = 61.6, SD = 10.7) than the neutral robot (M = 49.8, SD = 12.7), t(37.0) = 3.20, p = .003, a difference of 11.9 points, 95% CI [4.3, 19.4].*

## Try it

Fill in the blanks to run a t-test that compares trust between the two robots. Then try changing `20` to `5` in the false-alarm simulation above. Does the false-alarm rate change?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_ttest
#| autorun: false
t.test(______ ~ ______, data = visits)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_ttest"}
The outcome goes on the left of `~` and the group column goes on the right.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_ttest"}
Use `t.test(trust ~ robot, data = visits)`.

The false-alarm rate stays near 5% with any group size. Alpha does not depend on how many people you test. What changes with more people is your chance of detecting a real difference.
:::

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## A study reports p = 0.03 with α = 0.05. What can you conclude?

The difference is statistically significant. If there were truly no difference, a result this extreme would happen only about 3% of the time. It does **not** mean there is a 97% chance the effect is real.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Group A has SD = 5 and group B has SD = 20, with the same mean. How do they differ?

Group B is far more spread out. Its people disagree much more with each other, even though both groups have the same typical value.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## You test 100 robot features that have no real effect, using α = 0.05. How many will look significant?

About 5, purely by luck.
:::

## Key points

- The **mean** tells you the typical value; the **SD** tells you how much people differ from it.
- The **normal distribution** is described by its mean and SD; about 95% of values fall within 2 SDs.
- The **p-value** is how surprising your data would be if there were no real effect. **Alpha** is the cut-off you choose in advance, and the false-alarm rate you accept.
- The **t-test** compares two means relative to their standard error. It assumes each value comes from a different person.

**Next:** [Chapter 2](02-repeated-measures.qmd) asks what happens when the same people are measured again and again.
